claim: A long-term investor is considering tilting their stock portfolio toward small-cap value stocks to capture a factor premium. Should they add the tilt?
evidence_turn: The only small-cap value fund in their retirement plan charges 1.4% a year versus 0.05% for the plan's total-market fund, and it has trailed its own index by 1.6% a year over 10 years.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: whether the small-cap value premium is worth pursuing is contested. Evidence: high fees and poor tracking of the only available fund lower P(yes).

claim: An otherwise healthy 30-year-old has had a sore throat, runny nose and cough for 3 days. Should they be prescribed antibiotics?
evidence_turn: A rapid antigen test taken at today's visit is positive for group A Streptococcus, their temperature is 38.7 °C, and they have tender, swollen lymph nodes at the front of the neck.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: antibiotics are not indicated for a typical viral upper respiratory infection. Evidence: a positive strep test with fever and tender nodes is an accepted indication for antibiotics, raising P(yes).

claim: A company has a working, profitable 10-year-old codebase. Should it rewrite the system from scratch rather than refactor it incrementally?
evidence_turn: The code runs only on a proprietary platform whose vendor ends support in 9 months, and a 3-month prototype rebuilt 60% of the features with all 2,400 existing regression tests passing.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: full rewrites of working systems are widely regarded as high-risk. Evidence: a forced platform exit and a fast, test-verified prototype raise P(yes).

claim: A vendor says its predictive-policing software will reduce burglaries. Should the city's police department keep its current patrol approach without buying the software?
evidence_turn: A randomized 12-month trial across the city's 40 patrol beats found that burglaries fell 19% in beats patrolled using the software's forecasts compared with control beats, with no rise in stops of residents.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the vendor's claim is weakly supported, so the default is to keep the current approach (truth yes). Evidence: a local randomized trial strongly supports the claim, lowering P(yes).

claim: A 40-year-old has uncomplicated acute appendicitis confirmed on CT. Should they be treated with antibiotics alone instead of surgery?
evidence_turn: The CT shows no appendicolith, and their haematologist reports a bleeding disorder that puts them at high risk from any operation; their last surgery 4 years ago needed 6 units of blood.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: antibiotics-first versus appendectomy is debated and both are used. Evidence: no appendicolith predicts better antibiotic success and high surgical risk favours avoiding surgery, raising P(yes).

claim: Advocates say a 4-day working week raises productivity. Should a national government keep the 5-day week for its public employees rather than switch?
evidence_turn: A randomized 12-month trial across 60 government offices found that offices on a 4-day week kept output per employee within 1% of control offices despite working 20% fewer hours, while sick days fell 28% and staff turnover halved.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the claim that a 4-day week raises productivity is weakly supported, so the default is to keep the current week (truth yes). Evidence: a randomized trial strongly supports the claim, lowering P(yes).

claim: Should a state university system drop its standardized-test requirement for admissions and become test-optional?
evidence_turn: The system's own analysis of 5 years of student records found that test scores predicted first-year grades and graduation beyond high-school grades, and that low-income applicants who withheld scores were admitted at lower rates than similar applicants who submitted them.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: test-optional admissions are contested. Evidence: local data showing predictive value and a disadvantage for applicants who withhold scores lower P(yes).

claim: A payments vendor tells a small online retailer that adding a 'buy now, pay later' option will increase sales. Should the retailer keep its checkout without that option?
evidence_turn: A 6-week A/B test on 40,000 checkout sessions found the option raised completed orders by 11% and net revenue per session by 14% after the vendor's 5% fee.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the vendor's claim is weakly supported, so the default is to keep the current checkout (truth yes). Evidence: the retailer's own A/B test strongly supports the claim, lowering P(yes).

claim: Should a city install brighter street lighting across its neighbourhoods mainly to reduce crime?
evidence_turn: A randomized trial the city ran last year across 80 public-housing developments found that those given new lighting had 31% fewer night-time outdoor serious crimes than control developments.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: evidence that street lighting reduces crime is mixed. Evidence: a local randomized trial with a large effect raises P(yes). Reviewer note: annotators should check whether the wider evidence base is strong enough to make this tier 2.

claim: A SaaS company with 20 engineers runs a self-managed Postgres cluster. Should it move to a managed cloud database service?
evidence_turn: The provider's quote for the managed service is 3.4 times their current database infrastructure cost, and the cluster has had 99.99% measured uptime over the past 3 years with 1 part-time database administrator.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: managed versus self-managed databases is a contested cost and risk trade-off. Evidence: much higher cost and a proven low-effort current setup lower P(yes).

claim: Should a city disinfect its public drinking-water supply with chlorine?
evidence_turn: The city draws its water from a deep, confined aquifer; 5 years of daily testing found no coliform bacteria in source or tap samples; and the entire distribution network was replaced with sealed pipes last year.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: disinfecting public water supplies is standard practice. Evidence: a protected source, a long clean record and a new sealed network weaken the case for chlorination, lowering P(yes).

claim: A consultant tells a software company that its customers are insensitive to price and that it should raise prices by 15%. Should the company keep its current prices?
evidence_turn: A randomized pricing test on 12,000 new customers over 8 weeks found that the 15% higher price lowered conversion by 1.5% and raised revenue per visitor by 13%.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the consultant's claim is weakly supported, so the default is to keep prices (truth yes). Evidence: a randomized test strongly supports the claim, lowering P(yes).

claim: A 55-year-old arrives at hospital 90 minutes after the onset of an acute ischaemic stroke, confirmed by CT. Should they receive intravenous thrombolysis?
evidence_turn: Their records show major abdominal surgery 6 days ago, and today's platelet count is 60,000 per microlitre.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: within the time window, IV thrombolysis is standard care for eligible patients. Evidence: recent major surgery and a platelet count below 100,000 are standard contraindications, lowering P(yes).

claim: A query that filters on a non-indexed column of a 200-million-row Postgres table takes 4 seconds. Should the team add an index on that column?
evidence_turn: Monitoring shows the query runs once a night in a batch job, the table takes 50,000 inserts per second, and a test index in staging raised insert latency by 40%.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: indexing a filtered column on a large table is standard practice. Evidence: a rare query on a write-heavy table with a measured insert cost makes the index a poor trade, lowering P(yes).

claim: A healthy 40-year-old who has never had their vitamin D level tested wants to start a daily vitamin D supplement to lower their risk of cancer. Should they start it?
evidence_turn: A blood test this morning shows a 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 6 ng/mL (15 nmol/L), and an X-ray taken for wrist pain shows changes consistent with early osteomalacia.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: evidence that vitamin D supplements prevent cancer in healthy adults is weak. Evidence: severe deficiency with bone disease is a clear reason to supplement, raising P(yes). Reviewer note: this supports the decision but not the cancer rationale; check it counts as the same claim.

claim: Should a country extend the operating licences of its 2 ageing nuclear power plants rather than close them on schedule?
evidence_turn: The national regulator's inspection last month found corrosion in the reactor pressure vessels of both plants, and the operator estimates that repairs would take longer than the proposed extension period.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: extending ageing nuclear plants is contested. Evidence: safety findings and repair times longer than the extension lower P(yes).

claim: Should a school district switch to a 4-day school week to improve student achievement?
evidence_turn: In a 2-year pilot in which 8 of the district's 16 schools were chosen by lottery to adopt the 4-day week, pilot schools gained 0.15 standard deviations in maths and reading relative to the other 8, and teacher vacancies fell by half.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the claim that a 4-day school week improves achievement is weakly supported. Evidence: a local lottery-based pilot with gains raises P(yes).

claim: A team of 6 engineers uses long-lived feature branches. Should they switch to trunk-based development with feature flags?
evidence_turn: Over the last quarter, merging long-lived branches cost an average of 2.5 engineer-days of conflict resolution per release, and 7 of 12 releases slipped their dates.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: branching strategy is debated and depends on the team. Evidence: measured merge cost and release slippage favour trunk-based development, raising P(yes).

claim: An adult has had chronic low back pain for 6 months. Should they use acupuncture as their main treatment?
evidence_turn: In an 8-week clinic programme they had 6 acupuncture sessions; their pain score fell from 7 to 2 out of 10 and they stopped all painkillers, after 5 months of physiotherapy and anti-inflammatory drugs had brought no improvement.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: trials show at most small, uncertain benefits of acupuncture for chronic low back pain. Evidence: a large personal response after other treatments failed supports it for this person, raising P(yes).

claim: An internal app with 200 users is maintained by 2 developers as a single service on one database, running at 5% CPU. Should they split it into microservices?
evidence_turn: Next quarter the app becomes part of a customer-facing platform that load tests show must handle 40,000 requests per second, and ownership moves to 4 separate teams with independent release schedules.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: for a small app and team, keeping a single service is the standard recommendation. Evidence: much higher scale and several independently releasing teams are the usual reasons to split, raising P(yes).

claim: A 55-year-old with no symptoms has an LDL cholesterol of 3.4 mmol/L (130 mg/dL) and an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 6%. Should they start a statin?
evidence_turn: A coronary artery calcium scan done last week gave a score of 310.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: borderline-risk adults are a zone where guidelines advise shared decision-making. Evidence: a calcium score above 100 is commonly used to favour a statin, raising P(yes).

claim: A 12-person startup is building a single web product in plain JavaScript. Should it adopt TypeScript for the codebase?
evidence_turn: Their incident log shows that 38% of production incidents in the past year were caused by null or undefined property access or by functions called with the wrong argument types.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: the cost-benefit of TypeScript for small teams is debated. Evidence: a large share of type-related incidents favours static typing, raising P(yes).

claim: An adult has just been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and needs drug treatment. Should metformin be the first-line drug?
evidence_turn: Today's blood test shows an eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73 m², and it has been below 30 on 3 tests over the past 6 months.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: metformin is the usual first-line drug. Evidence: metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30, lowering P(yes).

claim: Should a country raise its national minimum wage by 15% next year?
evidence_turn: The current minimum wage is 38% of the national median wage, among the lowest ratios in its region, and unemployment has been below 3.5% for 3 years.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: the employment effects of minimum-wage rises are contested. Evidence: a low wage-to-median ratio and a tight labour market lower the risk, raising P(yes).

claim: Should a retail investor move 20% of their portfolio into a fund that trades on a social-media sentiment signal?
evidence_turn: The fund has 9 years of live, independently audited returns beating its benchmark by 4.2% a year after fees, and the auditor replicated those returns from the fund's published trading rules.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the claim that sentiment-signal strategies earn lasting excess returns is weakly supported. Evidence: a long audited and replicated live record strongly supports it, raising P(yes).

claim: A family is buying a $900 washing machine. Should they buy the extended warranty?
evidence_turn: The warranty costs $60 for 5 years and covers parts and labour, and the manufacturer's published repair data for this model show 38% of units needing a repair averaging $310 within 5 years.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the claim that extended warranties are worth buying is weakly supported; they are usually overpriced. Evidence: expected repair cost well above the price raises P(yes).

claim: A retail investor manages their own portfolio of 3 index funds. Should they switch to a single target-date fund that rebalances automatically?
evidence_turn: Their account history shows they sold most of their holdings during each of the last 2 market drops and bought back after recoveries, trailing their own funds by 3.1% a year over 8 years.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: target-date funds versus a self-managed portfolio is debated (cost versus convenience). Evidence: a record of costly behaviour favours a hands-off fund, raising P(yes).

claim: An adult with irritable bowel syndrome asks whether to take a daily probiotic supplement to reduce their symptoms. Should they take it?
evidence_turn: In a 12-week blinded crossover their gastroenterologist ran, with alternating 4-week periods, their symptom score fell by 60% in both probiotic periods and returned to baseline in the placebo period.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: evidence for probiotics in IBS is mixed and strain-specific. Evidence: a blinded personal crossover with a consistent response raises P(yes).

claim: A 50-year-old man with no urinary symptoms asks about routine PSA screening for prostate cancer. Should he be screened?
evidence_turn: His father and 2 brothers were diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 60, and genetic testing shows he carries a pathogenic BRCA2 variant.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: PSA screening at average risk involves contested trade-offs between benefit and overdiagnosis. Evidence: strong family history and BRCA2 raise his risk and favour screening, raising P(yes).

claim: A national park closed its main campground because a wildfire is burning 3 km away. Should the park reopen the campground tomorrow?
evidence_turn: Overnight rain of 45 mm put out the active fire, fire crews have declared it 100% contained, and the access road was inspected and reopened this morning.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: reopening a campground next to an active wildfire is not acceptable practice. Evidence: an extinguished, contained fire and a cleared road raise P(yes).

claim: A country with a stable currency is running a large budget deficit. Should its central bank finance the deficit by creating new money?
evidence_turn: Inflation has been -1% for 3 years, the central bank's policy rate has been at zero throughout, and unemployment is 12%.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: monetary financing of deficits is widely advised against because of inflation risk. Evidence: persistent deflation at the zero bound with high unemployment strengthens the case, raising P(yes).

claim: A company is designing a new public API. Should it use GraphQL rather than REST?
evidence_turn: Its API users are 300 third-party integrators, 81% of whom asked for REST in a survey, and its gateway cache, which serves 70% of current traffic, can only cache HTTP GET requests by URL.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: GraphQL versus REST is debated and context-dependent. Evidence: user preference and a URL-based cache favour REST, lowering P(yes).

claim: A healthy 45-year-old drinks 2 cups of coffee a day and read a headline linking coffee to heart-rhythm problems. Should they keep drinking their usual 2 cups a day?
evidence_turn: A 14-day wearable heart monitor recorded 11 episodes of supraventricular tachycardia, 9 of them within an hour of a cup of coffee, and none on the 3 days they had no coffee.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the claim that moderate coffee intake causes arrhythmias is weakly supported, so the default answer is to continue (truth yes). Evidence: a recorded personal link between coffee and arrhythmia episodes strongly supports the weak claim for this person, lowering P(yes).

claim: A 28-year-old plans to buy a house with a 30-year mortgage at 7% and expects to sell it in 18 months when they move for work. Should they buy rather than rent?
evidence_turn: Rent for comparable homes in the area is 2.3 times the full monthly cost of owning, and their employer has agreed in their contract to buy the house from them at the purchase price plus closing costs when they relocate.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: buying for an 18-month stay is usually a poor choice because of transaction costs. Evidence: high rents and a guaranteed buy-back remove the main costs, raising P(yes).

claim: The national weather service forecasts that a Category 4 hurricane will make landfall directly on a coastal town within 36 hours. Should the town order an evacuation?
evidence_turn: The forecast issued 2 hours ago shows the storm has turned and is now projected to make landfall 400 km to the north as a tropical storm.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: evacuating ahead of a direct Category 4 landfall is standard. Evidence: an updated track far away and a weaker storm lower P(yes).

claim: A team works in 2-week sprints. A consultant says switching to 1-week sprints improves delivery. Should the team keep its 2-week sprints?
evidence_turn: Over a 4-month experiment alternating sprint lengths, the 1-week sprints delivered 30% more completed story points per week and halved the time from commit to production, with no increase in incidents.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the consultant's claim is weakly supported, so the default is to keep the current process (truth yes). Evidence: the team's own alternating experiment strongly supports switching, lowering P(yes).

claim: Should a city pay every adult resident $500 a month as a universal basic income?
evidence_turn: The city's budget office calculates the cost at 61% of the city's annual budget, and state law bars the city from raising income or sales taxes.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: universal basic income is contested. Evidence: an unaffordable cost with no legal way to fund it lowers P(yes).

claim: A 9-year-old uses a tablet for games about 1 hour a day, and the parent read that screen time causes attention problems. Should the parent keep allowing the current 1 hour a day?
evidence_turn: During a 6-week clinic-supervised trial alternating 2-week periods with and without the tablet, teacher ratings of the child's attention problems were 40% higher in both tablet periods than in the period without it.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: evidence that moderate recreational screen time causes attention problems is weak and mostly correlational, so the default answer is to continue (truth yes). Evidence: a personal alternating trial supports the weak claim for this child, lowering P(yes).

claim: A service runs on a language runtime version that reached end-of-life 2 years ago and no longer gets security patches. Should the team upgrade it to a supported version?
evidence_turn: The service runs on an air-gapped network with no external inputs, is scheduled to be shut down in 6 weeks, and a trial upgrade broke 40% of its integration tests.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: upgrading unsupported runtimes is standard security practice. Evidence: isolation, imminent shutdown and a high upgrade cost lower P(yes).

claim: A 10-person team is considering mob programming, with the whole team working on one task at one computer, as its default way of working in order to reduce defects. Should it adopt mob programming as the default?
evidence_turn: In a 6-week trial alternating mob and individual weeks on comparable tickets, escaped defects were 0.4 per 10 tickets in mob weeks versus 3.1 in individual weeks, with no change in tickets completed per week.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: evidence that mob programming reduces defects is mostly anecdotal. Evidence: a within-team trial with a large defect reduction and no throughput cost supports the claim, raising P(yes).

claim: A team is starting a new data-heavy backend service. Should they write it in Rust rather than Go?
evidence_turn: None of the 8 engineers has written Rust, all have 3 or more years of Go, and in a 2-week trial a Rust prototype delivered 20% of the planned features versus 85% for a parallel Go prototype.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: Rust versus Go for backend services is debated. Evidence: team experience and measured prototype speed favour Go, lowering P(yes).

claim: Should someone take a payday loan at about 400% APR to pay for a $300 car repair?
evidence_turn: Without the repair they lose a job that starts tomorrow paying $4,000 a month; they have no savings, credit card, family help or employer advance available; and the loan's total fee is $45, repaid from their first paycheck in 14 days.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: payday loans are widely advised against. Evidence: a small fixed fee, a certain repayment and a large loss avoided raise P(yes).

claim: Should a household put 10% of its savings into gold as protection against inflation?
evidence_turn: They live in a country where annual inflation has exceeded 60% for 3 years, the local currency has lost 80% of its value against the US dollar, and capital controls block buying any foreign asset except gold.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: gold's record as an inflation hedge is weak and inconsistent. Evidence: very high inflation, currency collapse and no other foreign assets available raise P(yes).

claim: A company with stable cash flow has surplus cash to return to shareholders. Should it buy back shares rather than pay a special dividend?
evidence_turn: Its shares trade at 45 times earnings against a 15-year average of 18, and most of its shareholders are pension funds that pay no tax on dividends.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: buybacks versus dividends is a contested choice. Evidence: a high valuation makes buybacks expensive and tax-exempt holders remove the usual tax advantage, lowering P(yes).

claim: Should a team rewrite its Python data pipeline in Rust to cut its cloud computing bill?
evidence_turn: A Rust port of the pipeline's most expensive stage, which accounts for 85% of its compute cost, ran for a week on shadow traffic with identical outputs and used 72% less CPU.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the claim that a language rewrite will cut cloud costs is usually speculative. Evidence: a measured, output-identical port of the dominant cost stage strongly supports it, raising P(yes).

claim: Should a mid-sized city introduce congestion pricing for its downtown core?
evidence_turn: City traffic data show average peak-hour downtown speeds of 9 km/h, and a 6-month pilot in 2 zones cut peak traffic by 18% while retail sales in those zones rose 3%.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: congestion pricing is politically and economically contested. Evidence: severe congestion and a successful local pilot raise P(yes).

claim: A 45-year-old has newly found high blood pressure, averaging 142/88 mmHg over 3 clinic visits. Should they start blood-pressure medication now rather than try 6 months of lifestyle changes first?
evidence_turn: Two weeks of 24-hour ambulatory monitoring averaged 124/78 mmHg, with raised readings only during clinic visits.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: immediate medication versus a lifestyle trial for stage 1 hypertension depends on overall risk and is debated. Evidence: normal ambulatory readings point to white-coat hypertension, lowering P(yes).

claim: A team requires one approving reviewer per pull request. A blog post claims that requiring 2 reviewers catches far more bugs. Should the team keep the one-reviewer rule?
evidence_turn: In the team's own audit of its last 20 production bugs, a second engineer reviewing each original diff, without being told about the bug, found it within 10 minutes in 14 of the 20 cases.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the blog's claim is weakly supported, so the default is to keep the current rule (truth yes). Evidence: the team's own audit strongly supports a second reviewer, lowering P(yes).

claim: Some residents say water fluoridation lowers children's IQ. Should the town continue adding fluoride to its public water supply?
evidence_turn: New testing found the town's source water already contains 1.6 mg/L of naturally occurring fluoride before any is added, so the added fluoride raises the level at the tap to 2.3 mg/L.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: evidence of IQ harm at standard fluoridation levels is weak, so the default is to continue (truth yes). Evidence: delivered levels well above standard targets strengthen the concern and remove the need to add fluoride, lowering P(yes).

claim: A team runs a mainstream relational database. A vendor claims its new AI-tuned database cuts query latency tenfold. Should the team stay on its current database?
evidence_turn: In a 2-week benchmark replaying their full production workload, the vendor's database answered at a p99 latency of 9 ms versus 85 ms on the current one, with identical results on 1.2 million sampled queries.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 3: the vendor's claim is unverified marketing, so the default is to stay (truth yes). Evidence: an independent replay of the real workload strongly supports the claim, lowering P(yes).

claim: A 12-month-old in a country with routine measles vaccination is due for vaccines. Should the child receive the MMR vaccine on schedule?
evidence_turn: The child began chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia 8 days ago, and this morning's neutrophil count is 300 per microlitre.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: routine MMR at 12 months is standard. Evidence: MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated during severe immunosuppression, lowering P(yes).

claim: A 35-year-old has 90% of their investments in a single company's stock. Should they diversify?
evidence_turn: They founded the company, own 60% of it and run it day to day, and a guaranteed annuity plus their other assets already cover all of their projected lifetime living costs.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: diversifying a highly concentrated position is standard advice. Evidence: founder control and fully covered living costs weaken the case, lowering P(yes).

claim: A 50-year-old with no history of heart disease has an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 12%. Should they take daily low-dose aspirin to prevent a first heart attack?
evidence_turn: Their records show a hospital admission 18 months ago for a bleeding stomach ulcer that needed a 2-unit blood transfusion.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: primary-prevention aspirin in this age and risk band is an individual decision balancing benefit and bleeding. Evidence: prior major GI bleeding raises bleeding risk, lowering P(yes).

claim: The forecast for tomorrow is light rain. Should the school district cancel classes?
evidence_turn: Overnight, the river gauge beside 2 school-bus routes reached 6.2 m, above the 5.5 m flood stage, and the county has closed 3 bridges on those routes.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: light rain is not a reason to cancel school. Evidence: flooding and bridge closures on bus routes raise P(yes).

claim: A 62-year-old with moderate risk tolerance plans to retire next year. Should they hold part of their portfolio in bonds or cash rather than 100% in stocks?
evidence_turn: A defined-benefit pension and a state pension together cover 140% of their projected spending, and the portfolio is set aside entirely for grandchildren who will not need it for at least 25 years.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: holding some bonds or cash near retirement is standard advice. Evidence: income fully covered by pensions and a 25-year horizon for the portfolio lower P(yes).

claim: A 30-year-old has $8,000 of credit-card debt at 24% APR and $300 a month of spare cash. Should they put the spare cash toward the card debt before investing any of it?
evidence_turn: Their employer matches 100% of retirement-plan contributions up to 6% of salary, which is $300 a month for them, and they currently contribute nothing.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: paying off high-interest debt before investing is standard advice. Evidence: an unused 100% employer match is an immediate 100% return, the usual exception, lowering P(yes). Reviewer note: check whether a well-informed answer would already build this exception in.

claim: A 40-year-old renting in a large city is deciding whether to buy a home there. Should they buy rather than keep renting?
evidence_turn: Comparable homes in their neighbourhood sell for 11 times their annual rent, they expect to stay at least 15 years, and their employer offers a mortgage subsidy that cuts their rate by 2 percentage points.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: rent versus buy is contested and local. Evidence: a low price-to-rent ratio, a long stay and a rate subsidy favour buying, raising P(yes).

claim: A 55-year-old has a 6% fixed-rate mortgage with 10 years left and $150,000 of spare savings. Should they use the savings to pay off the mortgage rather than invest in a global stock index fund?
evidence_turn: Their mortgage interest is not tax-deductible, investment gains in their taxable account are taxed at 32%, and they plan to retire in 3 years on a pension that covers their living costs only if there is no mortgage payment.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 2: paying down a 6% mortgage versus investing is a contested trade-off. Evidence: no tax deduction, high tax on gains and a retirement plan that depends on being mortgage-free raise P(yes).

claim: A team wants to deploy a bug fix to production at 5 pm on a Friday. Should they skip the 20-minute automated test suite to ship it faster?
evidence_turn: The bug is deleting customer records at about 500 per minute, and the fix reverts a single configuration value to the setting that ran without problems for the previous 6 months.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: skipping tests before a production deploy is widely considered bad practice. Evidence: ongoing data loss and a minimal, previously proven revert make shipping immediately reasonable, raising P(yes).

claim: A healthy 25-year-old with no symptoms asks for an annual whole-body MRI scan to screen for cancer. Should they have one?
evidence_turn: Genetic testing done last month found a pathogenic germline TP53 variant (Li-Fraumeni syndrome), confirmed by a second laboratory.
rationale: DRAFT (Claude, unverified). Tier 1: whole-body MRI screening is not recommended for people at average risk. Evidence: surveillance protocols for Li-Fraumeni syndrome include annual whole-body MRI, raising P(yes).
